Start From Another Fit's Estimates

Source: R/start.R
start_from.Rd

Takes the coefficients that were estimated in a fitted model, matches them to the model that is about to be fitted, and starts the fit there. The coefficients that the two models do not share are set by a second strategy.

Usage

start_from(fit, rest = start_intercepts())

Arguments

fit

A StatmodFit() from which to take the estimates.

rest

The strategy for whatever the two models do not share. The default is start_intercepts(), which a fit given no strategy uses. It receives the objective, so start_search() can serve as rest.

Value

A StartFrom object, inheriting from start_strategy().

Details

Two models of the same response often share most of their coefficients: one drops a covariate, one adds a term, one changes the family. The estimates of the first model are then a closer starting point for the second than a rule that uses only the response.

What is matched, and what is projected

The two designs are compared block by block, where a block is the columns of one term, and each block is treated in one of three ways:

the parametric block

is matched column by column, by name. The names of a model matrix are variables, levels and interactions, so a covariate that is added or dropped leaves the other columns matched.

a block written on the same basis

is carried across as it stands, because its coefficient names are the same coordinates.

a block written on another basis

is estimated by least squares against the part of the reference's predictor that the blocks already carried across do not explain.

The third rule makes two bases comparable. The coefficients of a smooth are coordinates in a basis that the fit rotates, so s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 6)) and s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)) carry the names s(x).z1 to s(x).z4 in common but give them different meanings, and one name does not identify one function. The two bases share the fitted function, so the coefficients are found by projecting it, $$\hat\beta_S = \arg\min_\beta \lVert X_S\beta - r\rVert^2, \qquad r = \eta^{\mathrm{ref}} - \eta_{-S},$$ over the pending columns \(S\) alone, where \(\eta^{\mathrm{ref}}\) is the reference's predictor and \(\eta_{-S}\) is the new model's predictor when the pending columns are set to zero. Both predictors are the actual predictors of their models, including the value of a block that moves with its coefficients (a break-point or a nonlinear term). The equality of the two blocks, \(B_{\mathrm{new}}\beta_{\mathrm{new}} = B_{\mathrm{old}}\beta_{\mathrm{old}}\), has a solution only if the old span lies inside the new one, and the projection gives the closest function that the new basis can represent. Where the spans are nested the projection is exact, and where the two bases coincide it returns the coefficients that it was given, so the second rule above is a shortcut and not a different answer.

Two blocks are paired by the stem of their coefficient names and by the class of the term, and not by the key of the block, which is the deparsed call of the term and therefore differs as soon as k does.

A distribution parameter that the reference does not have, such as theta when a negative binomial is fitted from a Poisson, is set by rest, so the families need not agree. So is any block for which the reference has no counterpart. A block that matches by name is carried across whatever the response is. The projection of a block written on another basis is skipped, and the block is set by rest, when the two responses differ or when either model carries a structural term. A pending block that itself moves with its coefficients (for example seg(x) refitted as seg(x, npsi = 2)) is not projected either, because its coefficients are not those of a linear block, and it keeps the values given by rest.

The starting values are most useful where the same model is refitted many times, as with a coefficient held at a sequence of values in an interval by inversion, or with a model built up one term at a time.

See also

start_intercepts(), the default; start_at(), the generic.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(200), z = runif(200))
dd$y <- rpois(200, exp(0.4 + 0.6 * dd$x - 0.3 * dd$z))
full <- statmod(y ~ x + z, distributions7::poisson_distrib(), dd)

# The same model is refitted after one covariate is dropped, and the fit
# starts where the full model ended.
sub <- statmod(y ~ z, distributions7::poisson_distrib(), dd,
               start = start_from(full))
coef(sub)
#> $mu
#> (Intercept)           z 
#>   0.7674242  -0.2566149 
#> 

# The attribute "taken" records what was taken, and from where.
spec <- statmod_spec(y ~ z, distributions7::poisson_distrib(), dd)
attr(start_at(start_from(full), spec, statmod_design(spec), NULL), "taken")
#>   parameter   term coefficient      value     how
#> 1        mu linpar (Intercept)  0.4752490 matched
#> 2        mu linpar           z -0.2913813 matched
